svg.title: macOS · Import from Device · pairing code · 460×520
svg.desc: Mirrors Remote/ImportWindow.swift (enteringCode / connecting phases) over Shared/ProjectTransferClient.swift and Shared/CaptureRemotePairing.swift. The six digits shown in Projects on the serving device (iOS/projects.sharing.portrait.svg) are typed here. The code is never the key: it is stretched with HKDF-SHA256 into a TLS-PSK, under a PURPOSE-SCOPED salt ("com.regularsteven.letslapse.transfer.v1") so a code minted for the camera remote cannot be replayed against the library and vice versa — CaptureRemotePairing.derivedKey/parameters take the salt as a defaulted argument, leaving the capture link's wire behaviour bit-identical. The same call also asks for transfer-shaped TCP: keepalive 20/3/5 instead of the control link's 5/2/2, because 5/2/2 tears down a healthy forty-minute pull the moment a congested network stalls it, and Nagle is left ON since bulk chunks fill segments by themselves. THE TRAP THIS SCREEN IS BUILT AROUND: a wrong code never fails the client. It surfaces as -9846 bad MAC on the SERVER's first read and this side sits in .preparing forever — verified again for this link on 2026-08-27, and previously for the camera remote. So the client runs LocalNetworkTransport's 8-second timeout verbatim and reports "Incorrect code — try again" rather than leaving a window that does nothing. The last line is not decoration: one code opens the whole library, not the project you were looking at, and the serving side says the same thing. Connecting state (drawn as a variant of this file's own button): the field disables, the button reads "Pairing…" and a small spinner sits beside it. Verified 2026-08-27; staged with LL_TRANSFER=<6-digit code>, which types the real code rather than bypassing it.

g.text: Shown in Projects on iPhone 17 Pro, while sharing is on.
The code grants access to every project on that device, not just one.
